chunks: The narration of Zur‘ah from Samā‘ah: “Seventy verses.”

As for what he mentioned in his statement, “except for four surahs of it,” he does not recite them until he attains taharah (ritual purity), and they are: the Surah of Sajdah of Luqmān, Hā Mīm al-Sajdah, al-Najm Idhā Hawā, and Iqra’ bi-Ismi Rabbika.

The basis in this is what he mentioned in his statement, because in these surahs there is an obligatory sajdah, and sajdah is not permissible except for one who is pure from impurities, without disagreement.
And this is also indicated by [other evidence].

key_terms.أَرْبَعَ سُوَرٍ: Four surahs that are excluded because they contain obligatory sajdah.
key_terms.النَّجَاسَاتِ: Ritual impurities from which one must be free.
key_terms.سَبْعِينَ آيَةً: Seventy verses, referring to the amount mentioned in the report.
key_terms.سُجُودًا وَاجِبًا: An obligatory prostration required upon recitation of these surahs.
key_terms.طَاهِرٍ: A person in a state of purity.
key_terms.يَتَطَهَّرَ: To attain taharah (ritual purity) before reciting them.

ai.seo_question: Why should the surahs of obligatory sajdah not be recited until one has taharah (ritual purity)?
ai.summary: This passage explains a legal ruling concerning the recitation of the surahs containing obligatory sajdah while in a state requiring purification. It states that these specific surahs are not to be recited until one attains taharah (ritual purity), because their recitation entails an obligatory prostration. The text is significant in Shia fiqh for linking quran recitation with the rulings of ritual purity and obligatory sajdah.
